answer.summary: The article reports a qualitative study of 22 interviews with staff from 14 Horizon Europe projects (mostly food/agri-food, plus bioeconomy and one sector-agnostic project) on how stakeholder engagement tools are developed. It proposes four development phases (Purpose, Prototyping, Praxis, Post-project continuity) and two approaches, a project-focused approach (described as most common) and a user-focused approach. It argues that both EU structural R&I rules and project coordination shape these trajectories and that a user-focused approach fits mission-oriented and open-science policy. The sampling, coding steps and phase model are described clearly and the sample counts are internally consistent. However, the approach typology is not traced to individual projects, the causal and policy-level claims go beyond interview accounts from project staff, and end-user perspectives are absent.

issues.claim: The majority of the 14 projects follow a project-focused approach and the user-focused approach is only partial. These prevalence claims cannot be checked because the manuscript never assigns individual projects to either approach.

evidence.exact_quote: The majority of the projects examined in this study applied the project-focused approach in their work, wherein tools are developed as deliverables within a predetermined project logic.
evidence.location_hint: Discussion, 'Transitioning towards socially robust engagement tools', p.13

evidence.observation: Table 3 lists the two approaches only as four phase rows with two columns (project-focused vs user-focused). It gives no per-project or per-approach counts and no mapping of the 14 projects, so the 'most common' and 'majority' claims cannot be traced to the data.

issues.reasoning: The typology is presented as a central result and is used to draw conclusions about EU R&I, yet the reader cannot see how many projects or interviews fall under each approach or how classification was made. This limits assessment of how robust the typology is and whether the prevalence statements are supported.

issues.claim: Because user-focused tool development is uncommon, not involving stakeholders in tool development 'could result in less robust tools', and changes at structural and coordination levels are presented as the route to robustness.

evidence.exact_quote: Therefore, not incorporating stakeholder engagement in tool development could result in less robust tools.
evidence.location_hint: Discussion, 'Transitioning towards socially robust engagement tools', p.14

evidence.observation: Figure 1 presents a one-directional model in which the 'Missions approach' and 'Open science' (EU structural level) and 'Creative methodologies' and 'Alternative funding arrangements' (project coordination level) move a 'Project-focused approach' toward a 'User-focused approach'. The figure carries no empirical measures or sources for these links.

issues.reasoning: Robustness of tools is not measured in the study. The study also reports no tool-use or outcome data, and the Limitations section acknowledges that usability and long-term impact were not examined. The conclusion that engagement omission yields less robust tools, and the transition model in Figure 1, therefore go beyond the evidence collected from interviews.

issues.claim: Project-level and structural elements both 'influence EU R&I implementation' and jointly produce the two approaches.

evidence.exact_quote: this study indicates how both the project management and structural dynamics influence EU R&I implementation.

issues.reasoning: The study is cross-sectional and interview-based, and the accounts come from project staff describing perceived constraints. Influence of structural R&I rules or of project management on approach choice is not tested against alternative explanations (e.g., team expertise, funding history, partner composition). The causal wording in the conclusion is stronger than the design supports, and it also affects the policy recommendations.

issues.claim: Findings on stakeholder engagement and on how citizens and marginalised groups are valued describe the engagement processes themselves.

evidence.exact_quote: Between one and three project staff members were interviewed per project
user groups such as citizens were perceived as less knowledgeable, particularly about the feasibility of implementing certain changes.

issues.reasoning: All 22 participants are project staff, and the study has no interviews with end users, citizens or marginalised stakeholders, nor any triangulation with project documents or observation. Yet the paper makes claims about how citizens and marginalised groups are perceived and engaged. These are second-hand accounts, so the credibility and transferability of the claims about user groups are limited and the manuscript does not acknowledge this clearly.

issues.claim: The coding process was rigorous. Two authors coded independently and then combined codes to yield 46 codes and four phases.

evidence.exact_quote: After this, the first and second authors compared their codes and combined similar codes.
This resulted in 46 codes assigned to 257 pieces of text.

issues.reasoning: The manuscript gives no codebook or code list, no description of how disagreements were resolved beyond 'most were eventually integrated', and no reflexive or confirmability statement. The four-phase model is therefore difficult to audit from the text alone. The data-availability statement offers only anonymised raw transcripts on request, and I cannot judge whether a fuller coding frame exists elsewhere, since external resources are not part of this material.

answer.overall_assessment: The paper addresses a relevant gap with a clearly described qualitative design and internally consistent sample counts (9 agri-food, 4 bioeconomy, 1 sector-agnostic project; 17 approached, 3 excluded). Its main limitations concern transparency and inference. The project-focused versus user-focused typology is not traced to individual projects, and the coding frame is not shown. Causal and policy claims about structural influence, tool robustness and the transition model in Figure 1 exceed what staff-only interviews can support. Perspectives of end users and marginalised stakeholders are absent, though the paper discusses them. The findings are plausible as exploratory insight, but they need more explicit calibration and transparency before they can support the stated recommendations.
